opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes from listening to what people are actually trying to do with the models. We work closely with enterprise customers and developers, and you quickly see where things break: maybe the model isn't reliable enough at calling functions, or it struggles with long documents, or it doesn't reason well enough on a multi-step task. Those pain points tell you a lot about where to invest.

There's also a research side. Some capabilities are foundational and unlock many others. Reasoning is a good example. If the model gets better at reasoning, it gets better at code, math, agentic tasks, and almost everything downstream. So we try to prioritize capabilities with that kind of leverage, rather than chasing every single benchmark.

And then there's efficiency, which has always been part of our DNA. It's not only about adding a capability. It's about adding it in a way that keeps the model fast and cheap enough to deploy, sometimes even on-premise or on smaller hardware. A capability that only works in a huge model that nobody can afford to run is much less useful to our customers.

So it's a mix of these three things: what users need, what has the most leverage scientifically, and what we can deliver efficiently. Very often the most impactful work isn't a flashy new feature. It's making the existing capabilities much more robust, so people can actually build on them in production.

r001.rationale: The response discusses enterprise customers’ needs generally, but does not say industry-specific capabilities are underprioritized in general-purpose model development.

r002.rationale: It mentions code as a capability that benefits from better reasoning, but does not characterize coding improvement as chiefly requiring data curation.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a mix of things, honestly. The first filter is just: what do people actually use the models for? We have a lot of signal from the API and from La Plateforme and from enterprise customers, and when you look at it, the overwhelming majority of usage is not some exotic capability, it's code, it's structured extraction, it's agents that need to call tools reliably. So a lot of our roadmap is just making those boring things really good, because that's where the value is.

The second filter is what we think of as the frontier of what a model should be able to do natively versus what should be done around the model. Early on, every new thing was a separate model: a code model, a vision model, an embedding model. Over time, the pressure is to fold those into the main model. Multimodality is a good example. We did Pixtral as a separate release first because it let us learn what the data pipeline needs to look like, how to do the interleaving, where vision hurts the text capabilities, and then once we understood that, it became something we integrate into the base models rather than a side project. Function calling went through the same cycle. Reasoning is going through it now.

The third thing is, frankly, what's feasible for us as a company of our size. We can't do everything at once. So we try to pick capabilities where we think the open-weights angle actually matters. If a capability only really works at the scale of a closed trillion-parameter model, it's less interesting for us than one where you can get something very good at 24B or 120B that people can run themselves or fine-tune. Long context is a good example. Being really efficient at inference is another, because for a lot of our customers the question isn't "can the model do this" but "can it do this at a cost and latency that makes sense in production."

And then there's a research component, which is less about capabilities and more about the recipe. How do we make the pretraining data better, how do we do RL at scale, how do we make the models more robust to the kind of messy inputs you get in agentic settings. Those don't show up as a "feature" in a release announcement, but they're what determines whether the next capability we add actually lands.

So it's less of a big strategic plan and more of a loop: look at usage, look at what the research tells us is becoming possible, be honest about what we can execute on, and then ship it as a separate model first if we need to learn, and fold it in once we understand it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses common use cases and enterprise customers, but does not identify industry-specific capabilities as underprioritized in general-purpose model development.

r002.rationale: It mentions improving pretraining data generally, but does not characterize better coding ability as mainly requiring coding-data curation.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is what people are trying to do with the models and where the models are failing. A capability can look impressive on a benchmark, but the question is whether improving it actually makes the model more useful.

Coding is a good example, because it’s not just about generating a function. You need to understand the context, follow instructions, and sometimes recognize that you’re missing information. So there are several capabilities that have to improve together.

And then you have to think about the cost of delivering that capability. If you make a model a little better but much slower or more expensive, that’s not necessarily the right trade-off. I would think about it as improving what users can reliably accomplish within the constraints they actually have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses user needs and model usefulness but does not identify industry-specific capabilities as underprioritized in general-purpose model development.

r002.rationale: It says coding requires several capabilities to improve together, but does not characterize coding improvement as mainly a matter of requisite data curation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is what people are actually trying to do with the models, and where the models fail today. Is it that they don’t know the answer, that they cannot reason through the problem, or that they need access to a tool? Those are different problems, and they don’t necessarily require the same solution.

For example, if you want a model to be useful for coding, generating a good function is only part of the task. It also needs to understand the existing code, use tools, run tests, and correct its mistakes. So I would think about the whole workflow rather than just adding a capability that looks impressive in a demo.

Then there is the question of efficiency. Can we make that capability work reliably in a model that people can actually deploy, with reasonable latency and cost? That matters a lot. A small improvement that makes a model useful for many more tasks can be more valuable than a very spectacular capability that is too expensive to use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses user needs and general workflows but does not identify industry-specific capabilities as underprioritized in general-purpose model development.

r002.rationale: It describes coding as requiring code understanding, tool use, tests, and correction, but does not characterize coding improvement as largely a matter of data curation.
